name: All-on-4

lead: All-on-4 replaces a whole arch of teeth with a fixed bridge held by four implants, two of them angled to avoid grafting. Teeth are usually fitted within about a day of surgery, giving a new, uniform smile. In looksmaxxing circles it is filed under hardmaxx dental work for people with failing or missing teeth.

Titanium implants fuse with the jaw bone, and the tilted rear implants use denser front bone and avoid sinus and nerve areas. Follow-up studies from the originating group report high implant survival over several years, though much early research was manufacturer-funded and independent trials are small.

paras: A bridge screwed onto the implants is worn full-time. It is aimed at tooth loss rather than facial change, and trials of framework materials and implant configurations are ongoing.
Reported issues include wear of acrylic teeth, bone loss around implants, infection and implant failure. Costs are high and vary widely by country.

chain: Four implants hold a full arch
angle.text: People with failing teeth choose All-on-4 to get a full fixed arch in a new, uniform smile, which looksmaxxing culture files under hardmaxx dental work. It is established dental surgery with high reported implant survival, aimed at tooth loss rather than facial change.

lead: All-on-4 is a prosthodontic treatment concept in which a full arch of missing or failing teeth is replaced by a fixed prosthesis supported by four dental implants, the rear two usually tilted so they can be anchored without bone grafting. The prosthesis is typically fitted within about 24 hours of surgery, so a patient can leave with a complete set of fixed teeth. "All-on-4" is a trademark of the implant manufacturer Nobel Biocare.[1] In looksmaxxing culture it is classed as a "hardmaxx" dental procedure because people pursue it to replace damaged or missing teeth with a new, uniform smile.

The concept was developed by the Portuguese prosthodontist Paulo Maló and colleagues and named in a 2003 study, building on earlier work on tilted and immediately loaded implants.[1][2][3] Published follow-up studies from Maló's group report high implant survival over several years, although much of the early research was funded by the manufacturer.[1][2]

Systematic reviews describe the approach as a predictable way to treat atrophic jaws for patients who prefer to avoid bone-regenerative procedures, and a review of patient-reported outcomes found high oral-health-related quality of life and satisfaction, while noting the limited quality of available studies.[4][5] Registry entries on ClinicalTrials.gov show that comparative trials of framework materials and implant configurations are ongoing; none of the registered trials examined here was designed around facial appearance as an outcome.

paras: The procedure replaces the teeth of an entire upper or lower arch, usually ten to fourteen, with a single fixed prosthesis attached to four implants. The two front implants are placed in the denser bone toward the front of the jaw, while the two rear implants are angled about 30 to 45 degrees so that they avoid the maxillary sinus in the upper jaw and the nerve canal in the lower jaw, which can allow treatment without grafting bone.[1][2] The implant heads emerge near the second premolar, so a molar can be cantilevered at the back of the bridge.[1]

A provisional prosthesis is typically attached on the day of surgery (immediate loading), and a definitive prosthesis is made later. Prosthetic teeth may be acrylic (PMMA) over a titanium bar or made of zirconia; the choice between the two is described as debated, with acrylic regarded as shock-absorbing and zirconia as more durable.[1] A newer variant adds a milled titanium bar linking the implants.[1] Planning commonly uses cone-beam CT scans, and digital design and CAD-CAM manufacture are now common.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes the approach as suited to patients with total tooth loss, teeth broken or decayed beyond repair, teeth compromised by gum disease, or jaw bone loss that rules out conventional vertical implants.[1] Alternatives include conventional dentures, treatment with more implants (such as All-on-6), zygomatic implants anchored in the cheekbone for severely atrophic upper jaws, and bone grafting before standard implants.[1][6][7]

Encyclopedia accounts trace the concept to Per-Ingvar Brånemark's osseointegration work from the 1960s and to later work on tilted posterior implants and immediate loading in the 1990s.[1][2] Maló is credited with a first patient in 1998 and a 2003 clinical study in Clinical Implant Dentistry and Related Research that named the approach "All-on-Four"; that retrospective study described immediate-function mandibular rehabilitation with Brånemark System implants.[2][3] Nobel Biocare commercialised it from about 2004, and Grokipedia reports FDA clearance of the immediate-function protocol in 2005.[2] One summary notes the view that the name was coined for an approach assembled from earlier techniques.[1] A 2010 paper described the maxillary version, and Nobel Biocare marked the concept's 25th anniversary in 2023, reporting more than 250,000 patients treated.[2][8]

A 2017 systematic review screened 728 articles, included 24 that followed patients for at least three years, and reported an implant survival rate above 99 percent for more than 24 months; it also noted that only one study reported a sample-size calculation and that follow-up was limited.[4] A 2021 update in Dental Clinics of North America, written by investigators of the concept, summarises complications and their remedies, cantilever and occlusion trends and risk factors for failure.[9]

Reported outcomes from the originating group include implant survival of about 98 percent at five years and about 95 percent at ten years in a mandibular cohort, with high prosthesis survival.[2] A 2022 systematic review of patient-reported outcomes covered eleven studies and 693 patients aged 55 to 71, with follow-up from three months to seven years, and found high oral health-related quality of life and satisfaction; it called for longer randomised studies.[5]

Acrylic prosthetic teeth on a titanium bar wear and need periodic replacement, and bone loss around implants may later require additional treatment.[1] Grokipedia reports long-term implant survival declining over 10 to 18 years in cohorts, with the figures drawn from the originating group.[2] As with other implant surgery, infection, bleeding and implant failure are recognised possibilities, and the 2021 update discusses technical and biological complications and patient risk factors.[9]

The procedure appears in lists of aesthetic dental options as a way to replace badly damaged or missing teeth with a complete, even set. Wikipedia reports average costs in countries such as Thailand, Mexico and Turkey of 50 to 70 percent below those in the US or Western Europe, which makes dental tourism a recurring topic.[1] The Wikipedia article carries maintenance tags for promotional tone, and it notes Nobel Biocare's ownership of the trademark and its funding of studies by Maló.[1]

A 2017 systematic review of 24 studies reported high implant survival over at least three years, while noting limited follow-up and sample-size reporting.[4] A 2022 systematic review of 11 studies (693 patients) reported high satisfaction and quality of life.[5] A randomised study of 36 patients with atrophic upper jaws compared fixed prostheses on two zygomatic and two conventional implants with the All-on-4 concept, measuring quality of life and satisfaction after one year.[10] Other randomised trials have compared digital and conventional impressions,[11] and digitally planned guided surgery with a traditional workflow with four-year follow-up,[12] and one short-term trial compared chewing efficiency and bite force with conventional dentures, fixed prostheses and milled bar overdentures on atrophied lower jaws.[13] A prospective study followed edentulous patients treated with a prefabricated bar system for immediate loading for five years.[14]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a number of small registered trials, mostly of prosthetic framework materials (PEEK versus cobalt-chromium or titanium) and marginal bone loss, and comparisons of All-on-4 with All-on-6 or zygomatic implants.[15][16][17][18][19][20] Registered enrolments are typically between 10 and 40 participants. A hybrid PEEK-acrylic prosthesis trial registered 37 participants.[17]

Maló treats first patient with the immediate-function protocol.[2]
